old: In the villages and families I've spent time around, a lot of what we're trying to "re-invent" with intentional community is just done. Land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc. all go through the extended family and local memory, alongside the formal systems. Nobody has to announce a workshop called "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging," because an aunt has already given three people a task.

old: In March 2026, Sénégal passed [Law No. 2026-08](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/resources/law-no-2026-08-of-march-27-2026-amending-article-319-of-law-no-65-60-of-july-21-1965/), which raised the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to five to ten years in prison. It also makes public "apology" for homosexuality a crime, and certain financing or support meant to promote it. And that's on top of the arrests, rejection by family, harassment, assault and mob violence that were already happening. Some people say that once homosexuals are arrested they're actually protected in jail, because the mob can't get at them. I'm not going to praise communal belonging while ignoring the people who survive it by hiding who they are, or by leaving.
new: Sénégal passed a law in March 2026 ([Law No. 2026-08](https://www.humandignitytrust.org/resources/law-no-2026-08-of-march-27-2026-amending-article-319-of-law-no-65-60-of-july-21-1965/)) that increased the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to 5 to 10 years in prison, and it also made public "apology" for homosexuality a crime, along with certain financing or support meant to promote it. old: So yes, a society can be spiritually alive, generous, funny and super communal. It can also be cruel to people who break its categories. Both at once, which is hard to take in. Community isn't automatically freeing, then. It depends on who gets to belong without having to pretend.

old: One strange leftover of the old communal system is what people call the "Black Tax." If you make any money at all, you're expected to support your parents, your siblings, school fees, medical bills, funerals, whoever else the family's carrying. I understand the instinct, though. In the ancestral way of doing things, nobody made it alone. The people who fed you, raised you, housed you and protected you had a real claim on whatever you made of yourself later. So sharing was how the whole organism survived. Nobody thought of it as charity.
new: Then there's the so-called "Black Tax," a legacy of the old communal system: if you've got any money at all, you're expected to share it with your parents, your siblings, to pay school fees, medical bills, funerals, etc. I understand the instinct. In the ancestral way of doing things nobody made it alone, and the people who fed and raised you had a real claim on whatever you made of yourself later. So why not share in return? It was the most natural thing to do, and that's how the whole organism survived (nobody thought of it as charity).
source: Emulate round b t03 A and B

old: Today it can be soul destroying, because the obligation is still there but most of the communal life that held it up is gone. People don't share the land, the work, the childcare, the food and the daily belonging the way they did, but whoever earns the cash can still be expected to carry everybody. They can hardly build any independence or long-term stability. How are they supposed to get ahead? And the relatives who get the money stay dependent, because the payments don't give them any real alternative. The ancestral ethic is still alive, just inside an individualistic cash economy now. It keeps people alive, and it eats away at both sides while it does.
new: The problem is that it can be very soul destroying in today's world. The obligation is still there, but most people no longer live close enough to share land, work, childcare, food etc. and feel part of a larger whole, while whoever earns the cash can still be expected to carry everybody. So it's hard for them to become independent or build any long-term stability. How are they supposed to get ahead? And yet the relatives stay dependent, because the payments don't give them a real alternative. So the ancestral ethic carries on inside the individualistic cash economy, keeping people alive but gnawing at both sides.
why: A's sentences; the published obligation that survived the communal life holding it up, the earner expected to carry everybody, "dependent" (A: "a position of continued dependency"), the payments that don't create an alternative, and "both sides" (A: "gnawing at them")

old: It's also the boundary problem any money-free commune runs into. Life inside can go without cash, but taxes, hospitals, visas, school fees, family obligations, imported tools, etc. all still come with a price in money. And no, that doesn't mean bringing individual wages back inside! It means somebody has to handle all that, and the group has to decide how much shared cash to keep for it. And how do you stop access to outside money from turning into a new status hierarchy?
new: It's also one of the thorny boundary issues of living without money inside a money-based society. Life inside the commune can go without cash, but you'll still need money for taxes, hospital bills, visas, school fees, family obligations, buying in tools etc. That doesn't mean going back to individuals working for wages and bringing them into the commune, but it does mean someone has to handle it! Who's that going to be? And the commune has to work out how much shared cash it keeps for these things, and how to stop access to outside money from creating a new status hierarchy.
why: A's sentences; the published cashless inside, "family obligations" (A: "'Black Tax'"), who handles it (A: "someone has to do it!"), the shared cash and the status hierarchy that outside money can create; the break is the question "Who's that going to be?" (march r3: no break in either reading)

old: Outside work complicates that boundary too, and it starts before there's a common purse. Cash is only part of what it brings in. There's another schedule, another status system and social world, other loyalties, and often new habits of consumption. That's a lot to bring home from a job! In the first stage, whoever works outside gives the commune an agreed share, but the money can't buy them out of doing their share of the communal work, or buy extra political authority. And the group has to watch for outside jobs draining the people and skills it needs to build shared livelihoods. Otherwise the commune stays a dormitory for the cash economy, and the common purse never happens.
new: Another aspect of outside work is that it's not just money you're bringing into the commune. You're also bringing in a different schedule, a different status system, a different social world, different loyalties, different consumption habits etc. etc. And you can't exactly leave all that at the door, can you? In the first stage, where some people work outside and contribute an agreed share, it's really important that they can't use the money to buy their way out of communal work, or to buy a greater say in the political system. It's also important that outside jobs don't drain the energy and skills out of the people who could be building the communal livelihoods. Otherwise the commune will never develop a common purse, and it will stay a dormitory for the money economy.
why: A's sentences; "schedule" (A: "a different way of organizing your time"), "a different status system" (A: "different status differences"), "agreed share", "drain"; the break is a tag question that claims nothing new (A had none)

old: Zapatista communities ran into a version of this with migration. Some of them used to try to stop their young people from leaving, and now they negotiate with them instead: migrants can work elsewhere as long as they keep defined obligations to the community. The pull between leaving and belonging didn't go away. But now it's something the community can name and negotiate. I like that.
new: Some Zapatista communities used to try to stop their young people from emigrating, which is a version of the same problem. Now they talk it through with them instead: it's OK to go and work elsewhere, as long as the migrants keep certain defined obligations to the community. That doesn't make the pull between leaving and belonging go away, but at least now it's something they can name and negotiate. I like that.
why: A's sentences and its "I like that."; the published version of the same problem, the defined obligations, and the conflict that stays but can be named and negotiated (A dropped it)
